title: ISRO Ignites Gas Generator for LME-1100 Methane Engine, Its SpaceX-Style Bet on Reuse
excerpt: The October 9 test of the 1,100 kN LME-1100's gas generator moves India's Next Generation Launch Vehicle toward reusable methalox propulsion, with the full engine expected by mid-2027 and a 2,400 kN full-flow design completed behind it.
body:
• ISRO has completed the first ignition test of the full-scale gas generator for the LME-1100, its 1,100-kilonewton liquid oxygen–methane engine, conducted on October 9 and announced on October 16.
  • The LME-1100 is being developed for India's Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV); more than 70% of its components are made using additive manufacturing, with extensive participation from Indian industry.
  • The complete engine is expected to be ready by mid-2027.
  • ISRO has also completed the design of a larger 2,400-kilonewton methalox engine using full-flow staged combustion — the cycle SpaceX's Raptor uses — aimed at future crewed lunar missions.

India's space agency has taken a concrete step toward the class of reusable rocket engines that SpaceX made famous. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has successfully conducted the first ignition test of the full-scale gas generator for its LME-1100 engine — a 1,100-kilonewton powerplant that burns liquid oxygen and methane — as part of the development programme for the country's Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV).

The test was conducted on October 9, 2026, and ISRO announced the milestone on October 16. The gas generator is the component that drives an engine's turbopumps; a successful full-scale ignition is one of the gates an engine design must pass before a complete prototype can be assembled and hot-fired. ISRO says the complete LME-1100 engine is expected to be ready by mid-2027.

Why methane, and why now

ISRO's operational rockets burn solid propellant, hypergolic fuels or liquid hydrogen — none of them kind to reuse. Methane changes that calculation. A liquid oxygen–methane ("methalox") engine burns cleaner, leaves far less soot in its plumbing, and is therefore easier to inspect, refurbish and fly again. It is the propellant combination SpaceX chose for Starship's Raptor and Blue Origin chose for New Glenn's BE-4. Methane has a further advantage for deep-space ambitions: it can in principle be manufactured on Mars from local carbon dioxide and water-derived hydrogen, rather than carried from Earth.

The LME-1100 is also an industrial milestone at home. More than 70% of the engine's components have been manufactured using additive manufacturing — industrial 3D printing — with extensive participation from Indian industrial partners, a production model that cuts the part count and tooling burden of a traditional engine programme.

The bigger engine behind it

The LME-1100 is not the end of the roadmap. ISRO has completed the design of a more powerful 2,400-kilonewton liquid oxygen–methane engine built around full-flow staged combustion, the most demanding engine cycle in use: both propellants are routed through separate pre-burners before entering the main combustion chamber, maximising efficiency at the cost of complex plumbing, high pressures and severe thermal loads. SpaceX's Raptor is the prominent flying example. ISRO has not released the bigger engine's chamber pressure, specific impulse or throttling range, and construction and testing remain ahead. The engine is aimed at the heavy end of India's ambitions, including future crewed lunar missions; India has set a goal of landing astronauts on the Moon around 2040.

A programme building in stages

The gas-generator test follows a deliberate sequence. In January 2026, ISRO hot-fired a sub-scale thrust chamber with a single-element, 3D-printed injector head at the ISRO Propulsion Complex in Mahendragiri, sustaining ignition at a chamber pressure of 56 bar. Sub-system tests through the year have led to this month's full-scale gas generator. What remains is the hardest part: integrating turbopumps, thrust chamber and controls into a complete engine and proving it over repeated full-duration firings — the difference between a promising component programme and a flight-ready engine. If the mid-2027 readiness target holds, the NGLV's propulsion will be on track to move from design studies to metal-bending tests within this decade.
